props.title: Thieves Like Us
props.initialSlug: Young lovers turn to bank robbery in Depression-era South

sections.content: Robert Altman's Thieves Like Us masterfully reinvents the lovers-on-the-run genre pioneered by They Live By Night (1948), which was based on the same Edward Anderson novel. Where Nicholas Ray's earlier adaptation leaned into noir shadows, Altman strips away glamour for dusty Depression-era realism. The film follows escaped convict Bowie (Keith Carradine) and small-town girl Keechie (Shelley Duvall) through a doomed romance punctuated by bank robberies. Altman's signature overlapping dialogue and documentary-like shooting style make this feel more like watching found footage than a polished crime film.

sections.content: The film's use of period radio broadcasts creates an extraordinary sonic landscape that contextualizes the action within the Depression era. This technique would influence later films like American Graffiti (1973) and The Warriors (1979). Altman's decision to shoot on location in Mississippi lends authentic poverty-stricken atmosphere that stands in stark contrast to the more stylized crime films of the era like The Sting (1973).

What sets Thieves Like Us apart is its unflinching look at the banality of criminal life. Unlike the mythologizing of Bonnie and Clyde (1967), Altman shows bank robbery as unglamorous work done by ordinary people. The romantic relationship develops with awkward realism rather than Hollywood polish, presaging similar approaches in films like True Romance (1993) and Natural Born Killers (1994). sections.content: Altman's film arrived at a crucial moment when American cinema was reexamining its relationship with crime narratives. Between The Godfather (1972) and Mean Streets (1973), filmmakers were stripping away old glamorizations of criminal life. Thieves Like Us takes this further by refusing to even acknowledge its characters as particularly special or interesting - they're just people trying to survive.
